warmups.text: CPU memory bandwidth refers to the maximum rate at which data can be transferred between the CPU and the main memory (like a RAM chip). It is a critical factor in determining how quickly data can be accessed and processed by the CPU. A higher memory bandwidth means the CPU can fetch more data at once, which improves performance. For example, if a CPU has a memory bandwidth of 1000 MB/s, it can read and write 1000 MB of data per second, which is significantly faster than a slower bandwidth. This is especially important in applications that require frequent data access, such as scientific simulations or real-time data

CPU memory bandwidth refers to the maximum rate at which data can be transferred between the CPU and the main memory (like a RAM chip). It is a critical factor in determining how quickly data can be accessed and processed by the CPU. A higher memory bandwidth means the CPU can fetch more data at once, which improves performance by reducing the time spent waiting for data to be available. For example, if a CPU has a memory bandwidth of 100 GB/s, it can transfer 100 gigabytes of data per second, which is significantly faster than a slower bandwidth of 50 GB/s.

limitations: Llama uses HTTP streaming; original engine uses subprocess commands. End-to-end transport differs.
Native reset and greedy-mode setup are outside the clock; llama request includes cache-disabled request processing.
Original layer weights also have a persistent FP32 widened prefill cache; resident memory is not equivalent.
One process is live per visit; startup and warmup excluded. Background OS work and address placement uncontrolled.
All scores require separate numerical/quality review. Discovery is exploratory, never a performance claim.
